case.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017), Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention
case.excerpt: 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention. The attention used is called "Scaled Dot-Product Attention". The input consists of queries and keys of dimension d_k, and values of dimension d_v. The dot products of the query with all keys are computed, each is divided by sqrt(d_k), and a softmax function is applied to obtain the weights on the values. In practice the attention function is computed on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q; the keys and values are packed into matrices K and V. The matrix of outputs is computed as: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V   (Equation 1). The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention and dot-product (multiplicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to this algorithm except for the scaling factor 1/sqrt(d_k). Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. The two are similar in theoretical complexity, but dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice because it can use optimized matrix multiplication. For small d_k the two mechanisms perform similarly, but additive attention outperforms dot-product attention without scaling for larger d_k. The authors suspect that for large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients; to counteract this, the dot products are scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k). Footnote 4: to illustrate why the dot products get large, assume the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1; then their dot product q . k = sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i has mean 0 and variance d_k.
case.focus: Explain scaled dot-product attention (Section 3.2.1, Equation 1) using small, editable Q, K, and V matrices. Show similarity scores, normalized attention weights, and the output. Let the learner edit values and switch scaling on/off. Guide them through equal scores and a dominant score. Check that each row of weights sums to one and that the output equals the weighted sum of V. Do not train a Transformer.
case.audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows matrix multiplication and dot products but has not studied Transformers.

plan.concept: Scaled dot-product attention: scores QK^T/sqrt(d_k), row-wise softmax weights, output = weights · V.
plan.computation: Build Q (n_q x d_k), K (n_k x d_k), V (n_k x d_v) from editable matrices. Compute S = QK^T, scale by 1/sqrt(d_k) (toggle), row-wise softmax (max-subtracted) to get A, then O = A V. Also report row sums of A and the explicit weighted sum of V rows for the selected query row.
plan.visual: Left: heatmap of scaled scores S. Middle: heatmap of attention weights A with row sums. Right: heatmap of output O with the selected query row highlighted. Below: bar chart of weights for the selected query row.
plan.controls: n_q, n_k, d_k, d_v (sizes), scale toggle, query-row selector, and editable Q, K, V matrices.
plan.checks: Each row of A sums to 1; O equals A·V recomputed independently; softmax weights non-negative; scaling divides scores by sqrt(d_k).

spec.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Equation 1)
spec.hook: Edit tiny Q, K and V matrices and watch how dot products become attention weights and then a weighted average of the values.
spec.idea:
Attention answers a simple question: for each query, which keys look similar, and how much should I copy from their values? Similarity is measured by a dot product $q \cdot k$. A big dot product means the query and key point in similar directions.

Raw dot products can be large, and a softmax over large numbers becomes nearly one-hot with tiny gradients. Equation 1 therefore divides every score by $\sqrt{d_k}$ before the softmax. This keeps the scores in a range where the softmax is well behaved.

The softmax turns each row of scores into a probability distribution over the keys. Those weights are then used to take a weighted average of the value rows. So the output for a query is a blend of the values, with the blend determined by similarity.

Everything here is a toy: small matrices you type in by hand. No training, no learned parameters — just the forward computation of Equation 1.
spec.why: Scaled dot-product attention is the core operation inside every Transformer block. Understanding the shape flow and the role of the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor is the foundation for reading the rest of the architecture.

equations.caption: Equation 1: scores are the dot products of queries with keys, scaled by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$, softmaxed row-wise, then applied to the values.
Softmax turns a row of scores into non-negative weights that sum to one.
Footnote 4: if $q_i, k_i$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product has variance $d_k$ — hence the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling.

symbols.demo: shown in the score heatmap when scaling is off

spec.visual_caption: Three heatmaps in a row: scaled scores $S/\sqrt{d_k}$ (or raw $S$ if scaling is off), attention weights $A$ with row sums printed on the right, and the output $O = AV$. The inspected query row is outlined in each heatmap. Below, a bar chart shows the weights of that row over the keys.

explorations.title: Equal scores give uniform weights
explorations.change: Look at the weights heatmap and the bar chart without changing anything first, then try changing one entry of $K$.
explorations.observe: With all keys identical, every score is the same, so each weight is $1/3$ and the row sum is $1$. The output is the plain average of the three value rows. Change one key entry and the weights shift toward the matching key.
explorations.why: Softmax of equal scores is uniform: $e^{c}/\sum_j e^{c} = 1/n_k$. The output is therefore the mean of the value rows.

explorations.title: A dominant score and the role of scaling
explorations.change: Turn the scaling toggle off and on, and watch the weights heatmap and the bar chart.
explorations.observe: With scaling on, the first weight is large but not exactly $1$. With scaling off, the raw score $16$ dominates and the first weight becomes essentially $1$, so the output collapses onto the first value row.
explorations.why: Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks large dot products. Without it, the softmax saturates toward a one-hot distribution, which is exactly the small-gradient regime the paper warns about for large $d_k$.

pitfall.title: Softmax is over keys, not over queries
pitfall.text: The softmax in Equation 1 is applied row-wise to $QK^{\top}$, so each query gets its own distribution over the keys. Rows of $A$ sum to one; columns generally do not. Also note that scaling changes the sharpness of the weights but never changes their shape (number of rows and columns).
